```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, dpi = 160, dev = "ragg_png",
  out.width = "100%")
options(width = 85)
```

I recently published [Postal codes of Spain](https://dieghernan.github.io/codigospostales/), a project that estimates postal code areas from open data. You can explore the results on a map and download them as GeoPackage files. But how do we get from a collection of addresses to those polygons?

The main ingredient is a **Voronoi tessellation**. It sounds complicated, but the idea is simple: divide space according to the nearest point. Then clip those areas and merge the ones that share a postal code.

Let’s do it with **R**, **giscoR** and **sf**. To keep things manageable, we will use Slovenia and start with its capital, Ljubljana. Once we understand the steps, we will repeat them for the whole country.

> **Working draft.** This example explains the workflow. The polygons we create are not official postal boundaries, and this exercise does not validate the GISCO postal data.

## Before we start: what are we estimating?

The Spanish project uses CartoCiudad address points with their postal codes. It follows [Goerlich (2022)](https://doi.org/10.12842/WPIVIE_0322), who develops an idea presented by [Sánchez (2020)](https://www.nosolosig.com/articulos/asi-hice-el-mapa-de-los-codigos-postales-de-espana-con-sig-y-datos-abiertos). The [updated online version](https://www.uv.es/goerlich/Ivie/CodPost.html) describes the method in detail.

Here we will use the postal points distributed by GISCO, retrieved with **giscoR**. A representative point for a postal code tells us much less than thousands of addresses with that code. Detailed addresses can help the partition follow their distribution more closely, although proximity alone still cannot reproduce postal delivery decisions.

We have not established that Slovenian postal areas should follow municipal boundaries. Imposing those boundaries is a modelling choice for this exercise, inspired by the Spanish workflow, rather than a verified property of the Slovenian postal system.

## Getting the data

We need municipal boundaries and postal points. We will use the 2024 release of both datasets and cache the downloads locally. The first run downloads complete European files even though we request Slovenia only; subsequent runs reuse the cache.

```{r packages}
library(giscoR)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

```{r data}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
municipalities <- gisco_get_lau(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035, cache_dir = "data"
) |>
  select(LAU_ID = GISCO_ID, LAU_NAME) |>
  st_make_valid()

raw_points <- gisco_get_postalcodes(
  year = 2024, country = "SI", epsg = 3035, cache_dir = "data"
)
stopifnot(!is.null(municipalities), !is.null(raw_points))
```

We work in **ETRS89 / LAEA Europe (EPSG:3035)**, a projected coordinate system with coordinates in metres. This makes the 200 m and 50 m margins used later meaningful. Voronoi uses Euclidean distances in this plane, rather than road distances; the projection does not preserve every distance exactly either.

Before drawing anything, let’s see what we have.

```{r data-summary}
postal_points <- raw_points |>
  mutate(POSTCODE = trimws(as.character(POSTCODE))) |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE), POSTCODE != "") |>
  select(POSTCODE)

code_counts <- postal_points |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(POSTCODE, name = "points_per_code")

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Municipalities", "Downloaded points", "Points with a postal code",
    "Distinct postal codes", "Codes represented by one point"),
  Value = c(nrow(municipalities), nrow(raw_points), nrow(postal_points),
    nrow(code_counts), sum(code_counts$points_per_code == 1))
))
```

These counts describe the downloaded file. They do not establish whether every code is present or whether the coordinates are correct. Where there is only one point per code, the result will be a partition around those representatives rather than an estimate based on individual addresses.

Two points at exactly the same coordinates cannot generate separate Voronoi cells. We sort by postal code and keep the first point at each location, as in the original workflow. This is a reproducible tie-breaking rule, not evidence that the retained code is correct. The counts below show how many records we remove and how many locations have conflicting codes.

```{r duplicates}
postal_points <- postal_points |> arrange(POSTCODE)
coordinates <- as.data.frame(st_coordinates(postal_points))
conflicts <- bind_cols(st_drop_geometry(postal_points), coordinates) |>
  group_by(X, Y) |>
  summarise(codes = n_distinct(POSTCODE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(codes > 1)
duplicates <- duplicated(coordinates)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Duplicate locations removed", "Locations with conflicting codes"),
  Value = c(sum(duplicates), nrow(conflicts))
))
postal_points <- postal_points[!duplicates, ]
```

## Starting with Ljubljana

We select the municipality and the points inside it. Using `st_within()` avoids assigning a point exactly on a shared boundary to both neighbouring municipalities.

```{r city}
city <- municipalities |> filter(LAU_NAME == "Ljubljana")
stopifnot(nrow(city) == 1)
city_points <- st_filter(postal_points, city, .predicate = st_within)
stopifnot(nrow(city_points) >= 2)

background <- "#faf8f2"
ink <- "#203b47"
theme_set(theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = background, colour = NA),
  plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink, size = 19),
  plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = ink),
  plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey40", hjust = 0),
  plot.margin = margin(16, 16, 16, 16),
  legend.position = "bottom"
))

base_map <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = city, fill = "#e8e4d8", colour = ink, linewidth = 0.4) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA)

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = "#bd5137", size = 2) +
  labs(title = "Ljubljana: the starting point",
    subtitle = "A municipal boundary and points with postal codes",
    caption = "Source: Eurostat / GISCO, 2024")
```

### Building the cells

Each cell contains locations closer to its generating point than to any other point. Cell boundaries occur where distances to two points are equal. For this first demonstration, we keep all interior points, without the margins used in the national workflow.

```{r voronoi}
cells <- city_points |>
  st_union() |>
  st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(city))) |>
  st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
  st_sf(geometry = _)

base_map +
  geom_sf(data = cells, fill = NA, colour = "#bd5137", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, colour = ink, size = 2) +
  labs(title = "An area of proximity for every point",
    subtitle = "Cells still extend beyond the municipal boundary",
    caption = "Own elaboration using Eurostat / GISCO, 2024")
```

`st_union()` combines the points into a single geometry so we build one diagram. The `envelope` argument supplies a working extent; it **does not clip** the cells to the municipality. We need an intersection for that.

### Clipping and recovering postal codes

We should not assume that cells come out in the same order as the input points. We recover their codes with a spatial relationship before clipping them. Each cell must contain exactly one generating point.

```{r clip-cells}
point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, city_points)
stopifnot(all(lengths(point_matches) == 1L))
cells$POSTCODE <- city_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]
city_cells <- st_intersection(cells, st_geometry(city))

city_areas <- city_cells |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  st_make_valid()

city_colours <- setNames(
  hcl.colors(nrow(city_areas), palette = "Dark 3"),
  sort(city_areas$POSTCODE)
)
ggplot(city_areas) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = POSTCODE), colour = background, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_sf(data = city_points, shape = 21, fill = ink,
    colour = background, size = 2.4) +
  geom_sf_text(data = st_point_on_surface(city_areas),
    aes(label = POSTCODE), colour = ink, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = city_colours, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "From points to estimated areas",
    subtitle = "Cells clipped and merged by postal code",
    caption = "Teaching example · Not official postal boundaries")
```

Grouping by postal code with `summarise()` merges the geometries. With many addresses sharing a code, their cells would dissolve into one geometry, possibly with several separate parts.

## From one municipality to the whole country

We now repeat the operation for each component of each municipality. A municipality may have separate pieces: normalizing to `MULTIPOLYGON` and then casting to `POLYGON` lets us handle them independently, rather than automatically extending a code to another piece with no points.

```{r municipal-components}
components <- municipalities |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  mutate(component_id = row_number())
```

### Why use an inward margin?

In the Spanish project, we first select addresses within an inward margin of **200 m**. If none are found, we try **50 m**. This reduces the influence of points close to a boundary, where small mismatches between layers may affect their assignment.

These are project parameters, not universal values. We keep them here to explain that workflow, although they can exclude useful information when postal points are sparse. Goerlich describes a 20 m margin; the 200 m and 50 m choices belong to my implementation. Comparing other margins would be a useful next step.

```{r select-points}
select_points <- function(component, postal_points) {
  for (margin in c(200, 50)) {
    interior <- st_buffer(component, -margin)
    if (all(st_is_empty(interior))) next
    selected_points <- st_filter(postal_points, interior, .predicate = st_within)
    if (nrow(selected_points) > 0) return(selected_points)
  }
  postal_points[0, ]
}
```

The margin only selects points: the resulting areas cover the **original** component, not the smaller buffered geometry. If both attempts fail, we leave the component unassigned. We do not borrow the nearest point from outside the municipality.

### Three cases, one function

With no points, we keep the component and assign `NA`. If all selected points share a code, we assign that code to the whole component. We only need Voronoi when several codes are present.

```{r build-postal-areas}
build_areas <- function(component, postal_points) {
  selected_points <- select_points(component, postal_points)
  codes <- unique(selected_points$POSTCODE)

  if (length(codes) <= 1L) {
    component$POSTCODE <- if (length(codes)) codes else NA_character_
    return(component)
  }

  cells <- selected_points |>
    st_union() |>
    st_voronoi(envelope = st_as_sfc(st_bbox(component))) |>
    st_collection_extract("POLYGON") |>
    st_sf(geometry = _)
  point_matches <- st_intersects(cells, selected_points)
  stopifnot(all(lengths(point_matches) == 1L))
  cells$POSTCODE <- selected_points$POSTCODE[unlist(point_matches)]

  result <- st_intersection(cells, st_geometry(component)) |>
    group_by(POSTCODE) |>
    summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
    st_make_valid()
  result$LAU_ID <- component$LAU_ID
  result$LAU_NAME <- component$LAU_NAME
  result$component_id <- component$component_id
  result
}

result <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(components)), function(i) {
  build_areas(components[i, ], postal_points)
}) |>
  bind_rows()
```

### Handling unassigned areas

A component without points may belong to a municipality whose other components do have information. We recover its code only if the municipality has **one distinct recovered code**. This is an imputation from the available data, not proof that the municipality really has just one code.

```{r unassigned}
unique_codes <- result |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  distinct(LAU_ID, POSTCODE) |>
  add_count(LAU_ID) |>
  filter(n == 1)

unassigned_before <- sum(is.na(result$POSTCODE))
index <- match(result$LAU_ID, unique_codes$LAU_ID)
recoverable <- is.na(result$POSTCODE) & !is.na(index)
result$POSTCODE[recoverable] <- unique_codes$POSTCODE[index[recoverable]]
```

Finally, we repair geometries and keep only surfaces. Repairs can produce collections containing residual lines or points, which do not belong in an area layer. Dissolving by postal code also removes municipal boundaries between areas sharing that code.

```{r dissolve-areas}
keep_surfaces <- function(x) {
  geometry <- st_make_valid(st_geometry(x))
  geometry <- lapply(geometry, function(part) {
    if (!inherits(part, c("POLYGON", "MULTIPOLYGON", "GEOMETRYCOLLECTION"))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }
    surfaces <- suppressWarnings(st_collection_extract(st_sfc(part), "POLYGON"))
    if (length(surfaces) == 0L || all(st_is_empty(surfaces))) {
      return(st_multipolygon())
    }
    st_cast(st_union(surfaces), "MULTIPOLYGON", warn = FALSE)[[1]]
  })
  st_geometry(x) <- st_sfc(geometry, crs = st_crs(x))
  x[!st_is_empty(x), ]
}

unassigned <- result |>
  filter(is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  keep_surfaces()
postal_areas <- result |>
  filter(!is.na(POSTCODE)) |>
  group_by(POSTCODE) |>
  summarise(.groups = "drop") |>
  keep_surfaces() |>
  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON")
```

## The complete map

For the national overview, we colour areas by the first digit of their code. This is a visual grouping to keep the map readable, not a validated classification of postal regions. Unassigned components appear in grey.

```{r national-map, fig.height=7}
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = municipalities, fill = "#d5d2ca", colour = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = postal_areas,
    aes(fill = substr(POSTCODE, 1, 1)), colour = background, linewidth = 0.15) +
  geom_sf(data = unassigned, fill = "#727a80", colour = background, linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "First postal code digit") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Slovenia, point by point",
    subtitle = "Proximity areas clipped to municipal boundaries",
    caption = paste("Eurostat / GISCO, 2024 · Own elaboration",
      "Dark grey: unassigned areas · Estimated boundaries, not official", sep = "\n"))
```

## Checking the result

A good-looking map is not enough. We check that geometries are valid, assigned and unassigned areas cover the territory and there are no appreciable area overlaps. We allow one square metre for numerical differences in geometric operations.

```{r geometry-checks}
territory <- st_union(municipalities)
coverage <- st_union(c(st_geometry(postal_areas), st_geometry(unassigned)))
difference_m2 <- as.numeric(sum(st_area(st_sym_difference(territory, coverage))))
overlap_m2 <- as.numeric(
  sum(st_area(postal_areas)) + sum(st_area(unassigned)) - sum(st_area(coverage))
)
stopifnot(all(st_is_valid(postal_areas)), all(st_is_valid(unassigned)),
  difference_m2 < 1, abs(overlap_m2) < 1)

knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Codes with an estimated area", "Components assigned by municipal recovery",
    "Unassigned records", "Unassigned area (km²)",
    "Coverage difference (m²)", "Overlap (m²)"),
  Value = round(c(nrow(postal_areas), sum(recoverable), nrow(unassigned),
    as.numeric(sum(st_area(unassigned))) / 1e6, difference_m2,
    overlap_m2), 4)
))
```

These checks verify the geometry, **not postal accuracy**. We could cover an entire country with valid polygons and still have a poor approximation of its delivery areas.

We save the two layers separately so that unassigned areas remain visible.

```{r export-layers}
st_write(postal_areas, "postal-areas.gpkg", layer = "postal_areas",
  delete_layer = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
st_write(unassigned, "postal-areas.gpkg", layer = "unassigned",
  delete_layer = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)
writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), "session-info.txt")
```

## Back to Spain

We now have the full sequence: points, proximity areas, clipping and merging by postal code. The same structure works with much more detailed addresses, such as the CartoCiudad data used in my [Spanish postal codes project](https://dieghernan.github.io/projects/postal-codes-spain).

The quality of those addresses matters as much as the algorithm. With one representative point per code, Voronoi mainly maps distances between representatives. With address points, it can better approximate where addresses with each code are concentrated, while still knowing nothing about delivery routes, physical barriers or official boundaries.

This example does not compare its results with an independent postal source for Slovenia. Before using it for analysis, we would need to review coverage, coordinates, the relationship with municipalities and sensitivity to the margins. For now, it gives us a way to open the box and understand how the map is built.
